tagline: Social posts that move: a short animation over a design, exported as video.
verdictSummary: An animated social post is a design plus a small timeline: elements enter, hold and leave, and the whole thing renders to a five-second video. Building the timeline and the deterministic renderer is a real few days, because a preview that plays smoothly in a browser and an export that matches it frame for frame are two different problems. What you cannot rebuild is the library — animated templates are the entire reason people use this rather than a static editor.
coreLoopDIY: Lay out a design, give each element an entrance and exit with timing on a short timeline, preview it, and render an MP4 or GIF at the platform's exact dimensions.
whatYouLose: the animated template library and the stock video and photo allowance
the background removal and other one-click asset tools
team brand kits and shared asset storage
the built-in scheduler that posts what you made
whyPeopleStillPay: Because an animated template is a finished idea, and thirteen dollars for a thousand of them beats an editor where every post starts from an empty timeline.
notes: Animation is the angle, deliberately distinct from the static fixed-size social editor already in this catalogue — the timeline and the deterministic render are the whole build.
prompt:
Build an animated social post editor. Static design in, short video out.

Canvas: a fixed size chosen from platform presets (square, portrait, story, wide). Elements: text, image, shape, and a background (solid, gradient or image).

Timeline, which is the point of this build. Duration is short and bounded — 2 to 15 seconds. Each element carries:

- An entrance: fade, slide from a direction, scale up, or typewriter for text.
- A hold period.
- An exit: fade, slide out, scale down, or none.
- A start offset and durations for each phase.

Represent the whole animation as a declarative list of keyframes per element, evaluated by a single function of time. Both the preview and the renderer call that same function, which is the only way the exported video matches what the user saw. A preview driven by CSS transitions and an export driven by separate frame maths will always diverge, and the divergence is what makes homemade animation tools untrustworthy.

Easing: a small fixed set (linear, ease-out, ease-in-out, and one spring-like curve), implemented as explicit functions. No arbitrary bezier editor.

Preview: play, scrub, and loop, at real time, in the canvas. A frame counter and a time readout so timing can be discussed precisely.

Rendering: evaluate the keyframe function at each frame, draw to an offscreen canvas, and pipe the frames to ffmpeg. Export MP4 (H.264, even dimensions, correct pixel format for platform compatibility) and animated GIF with a generated palette. Show real progress and allow cancellation without leaving a partial file. Render in a background process so the editor stays usable.

Audio: an optional audio file trimmed to the animation length, with a fade at both ends. Ship no music.

Text auto-fit: text boxes have fixed frames and the type size scales to fit, so a typewriter entrance does not reflow the layout mid-animation.

Templates: a template is a design plus its timeline, saved as a file. Ship none; the first run walks the user through saving one from something they made.

Export check: warn before rendering if the output would exceed a configurable file-size budget, since every platform has a limit and discovering it at upload time is the usual failure.

Out of scope: a template or stock library, background removal, collaboration, scheduling or publishing, and any hosted rendering.

faq.q: Can I export my VistaCreate designs?
faq.a: As finished images and videos, which stay usable. There is no editable export, so designs are rebuilt — and animated ones in particular, since no export preserves the timeline as structure.

faq.q: Why evaluate one keyframe function for both preview and export?
faq.a: Because otherwise they drift. A preview built on CSS transitions and an export built on separate frame arithmetic will disagree about easing and timing, and the user finds out after rendering. One function called by both is the only reliable way to make what you see match what you get.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing. Rendering happens locally through ffmpeg, and a five-second 1080p clip takes seconds. Unlimited exports at no marginal cost is the clearest advantage over a credit-based plan.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Having something to start from. An animated template is a designed idea with the timing already worked out, and animating from scratch is a genuinely different skill from arranging a static layout. An empty timeline is a much emptier page than an empty canvas.
